1:
The opening word occupies the commentators before the psalm does. Augustine reports a dispute over the doubled Hallelujah — whether one of them closes the previous psalm — and declines to settle it against custom, which attaches the word to whichever psalm it heads; very few copies, and none of the Greek he inspected, place it at the end of the last psalm of all. Charles Ellicott treats the phrase that follows as a liturgical formula holding the place in the Jewish church that the Gloria Patri holds in Christian worship, its first appearance undatable but attested by the chronicler at the bringing up of the ark and again at the dedication of the temple, and spreading into general use after the Captivity.

Who wrote it, and when, is disputed. Adam Clarke reports that eminent commentators take it for a prayer of the captives in Babylon, confessing their fathers' sins and their own and asking to be gathered from the heathen. John Calvin notes that the first and last verses belong to the psalm David delivered to Asaph to be sung before the ark, so that this one has been ascribed to him. Delitzsch presses the same fact into an argument: since the chronicler already puts these verses in David's mouth, the psalm is no more Maccabean than the two before it, and the Psalter must already have been divided into five books marked off by their doxologies — from which he also infers that the closing benediction was read as part of the psalm even then. Ellicott finds another clue, that the tone of the fifth verse suggests the near prospect of good and so helps fix a date. Calvin also states its relation to the psalm before it: there God was shown more than a bountiful father, here the benefits are acknowledged turned to bad account — yet this is not reproof so much as confession offered to obtain pardon, which is why it opens with praise, to encourage hope.

Asked who can utter the mighty acts, Matthew Henry answers that they are too many to number and too mysterious to describe, and that not the angels can show forth all — which does not excuse us from doing what we can but should quicken us to do all we can. Gill notes that a Jewish commentator restricted the acts to Egypt and the Red Sea, and widens them to creation, providence and redemption. Ellicott takes the second noun as the technical term for a liturgical hymn and reads the verse as asking who is privileged to sing one, covenant loyalty conferring the privilege. C.H. Spurgeon turns the point on his own congregations: it is not fitting for a few to praise while the rest are silent, and if David were present where choirs carry all the singing he would turn to the people and tell them to praise the Lord.

The beatitude is read as habitual obedience. Henry has them adhering to the rules of wisdom and religion, just to God and men, steady at every turn. Gill offers two senses, either observing God's judgments on the wicked or keeping his statutes as the rule of life. Clarke sets the clause beside its Anglo-Saxon and old Scottish renderings to show how near the older English stands to our own, and concludes that those whose lives are not conformed to God's will have no happiness. At the prayer that follows, Clarke reports that several manuscripts and all the versions but one read the plural — remember us, that we may rejoice — and thinks this more agreeable to the context; John Wesley keeps the singular but has the psalmist speaking for the whole nation. Both gloss the seeing of the next verse as enjoyment rather than sight, and Gill expands the good of the chosen into blessings laid up for them, not any goodness of their own.
6:
The confession proper begins here, and the voices differ over whose sin it is. Adam Clarke keeps the generations parallel and distinct — our forefathers sinned and suffered, and we, like them, have sinned and do suffer. Charles Ellicott insists that the speaker and his own generation are included as much as the ancestors, and dates the psalm from the Captivity, when the national conscience — at least that of the nobler part of the nation — was thoroughly alive to the sinfulness of idolatry. C.H. Spurgeon makes the sharing formal: Israel was one nation through all time, so what follows is national rather than personal sin, and a people enjoying national privileges shared national guilt; men sin with their fathers when they make their own lives mere continuations of the follies of their sires. Gill traces the inheritance further back, to the corrupt nature derived from the first father of all. Matthew Henry reads the confession as seasonable because the church was in distress: we must justify God in what he brings on us, and the remembrance that former sins did not make him cast off his people is ground for hope that we shall not be utterly abandoned. Spurgeon notes that the confession is made three times over as a token of sincerity.

The first failure named is one of understanding, not of sight. Gill points out that they saw the plagues and had no heart to perceive what they were for — not merely the ruin of their enemies but proof that the God who wrought them was the only God — and remarks that the same slowness may be seen in the disciples of Christ. Keil and Delitzsch make it the root of everything that follows: falling away from faith in the promise, they forgot the works done to confirm it. The doubled mention of the sea is variously handled. Clarke reports a rabbinic reading finding two distinct faults in it: the murmuring against Moses when the water lay before them and Pharaoh behind, and then, once the water had parted, the fear of entering lest they stick fast in the mud; they provoked him at the sea and in it.

That God saved them nevertheless is referred by all the voices to himself. Gill denies any worth in the people and grounds the deliverance in the covenant and the name called upon them, adding that spiritual Israel is saved on the same terms. Clarke puts it compactly: there was nothing in them from which he could draw a reason, so he drew it from himself. John Wesley makes the vindication defensive: the name would have suffered blasphemous reproach had the people been destroyed. Clarke quotes a gloss from an old English psalter which retells the crossing in its own dialect and appears to suppose the sea divided into twelve passages, one for each tribe. At the rebuke of the sea Clarke observes that in this psalmist's descriptions everything has life: the sea is an animated being, which behaves proudly, is rebuked, and retires in confusion. Gill prefers the plain means, the east wind that drove the waters back; Wesley notes only that they passed as securely as on dry land.

The belief recorded at the close is not treated as a credit to them. Gill is explicit that it is noted to show the slowness of their hearts rather than to commend them: they believed on sight, as Thomas did, and the blessing belongs to those who have not seen and yet believe. Clarke says the same in six words: they believed just while the miracle was before their eyes — which sets up the reproach that they soon forgot. Delitzsch anticipates it, treating the singing at the sea and the forgetting as halves of one movement, the first principal sin beyond the water being an impatient murmuring about meat and drink.
13:
Matthew Henry calls what follows an abridgment of Israel's provocations, and notes that the apostle abridged it again for Christians, these things being written for our admonition. Keil and Delitzsch group the first three verses as one movement, the earliest of the principal sins beyond the sea being an unthankful and unbelieving murmuring over meat and drink. The haste is taken two ways: the margin reads that they made haste and forgot, which Henry treats as possibly two faults, their expectations running ahead of God's promises. John Gill and John Wesley fix the interval at three days, Adam Clarke at Marah. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as a hurry to get the Lord's mercies out of memory — they hasted to be ungrateful — a fault common still.

Gill is careful that the craving which follows is not natural appetite, which would not be criminal, but a voluptuous one; Spurgeon has them growing dainty, sniffing at angels' food, dwelling on the desire until it became a mania carrying away its rider. What God sent them divides the voices. Clarke reads it physically: they despised the manna as innutritive, God gave the flesh without a blessing, and they grew lean rather than fat on it. Wesley puts the leanness in the body, the desire to pamper it becoming the means of destroying it. Charles Ellicott prefers the Greek, Latin and Syriac reading, satiety rather than leanness, and observes that with the other noun taken as lust the verse falls into two parallel clauses — he gave them their request, and sent satiety for their lust.

On the envy of Moses, Spurgeon is most searching: they owed him everything and grudged him the authority he had to exercise for their good; if the meekest of men was envied, who can hope to escape it; and the envy was absurd, since Moses laboured hardest and bore most. They would snatch the sceptre from one, the mitre from the other. Gill supplies the claim behind it: Dathan and Abiram, being of Reuben, thought themselves better entitled as sons of Jacob's firstborn. Ellicott finds the objection in the title, the disaffected holding that holiness belonged to the whole congregation and was usurped by these two; and notes that Korah is passed over in keeping with the accounts, which distinguish both his attitude and his fate from theirs. Wesley reads the rebellion as aimed past Aaron at God, who had consecrated him.

At the calf Gill presses two aggravations: the figure was borrowed from the Egyptians, a people who had used them ill and whose judgments they had watched, and it was made at the mountain where the law against graven images had been given. Spurgeon notes that the ox is called a calf in scorn, never more legitimately used than against attempts to set forth the Invisible God, and turns the charge on the ritualists of his own day, whose worship appeals to eye and ear and nose. Wesley sharpens the exchange: an ox so far from feeding his people, as the true God had, that it must be fed by them. Ellicott uses the same verses as evidence of sources, the phrase for the place and the word for the likeness being Deuteronomic and showing that book was before the poet. At the last verse Ellicott offers an alternative to the usual explanation of standing in the breach, taken from the defence of a besieged town and adopted by Wesley: that Moses stood submissively before God in the breaking forth of his anger, the noun coming from the verb used of the Lord breaking forth upon the people, as the Greek seems to have read it. Clarke uses the word rendered chosen to enter a caution: it would be very difficult to show this word anywhere in the Old Testament refers to any man's eternal state, much less to unconditional election and reprobation.
24:
John Gill notes the sharpness of the charge that they despised the land: the spies owned it flowed with milk and honey and only judged the difficulties insuperable, so the contempt lay in refusing to go up at all. John Wesley makes it a preference, Egypt and the old bondage set above the promise. C.H. Spurgeon locates the root a clause later, in the unbelief: if we do not believe the Lord's word we shall think lightly of his promised gifts, and to prefer earthly things to heavenly is to prefer Egypt to Canaan. On the raised hand, Charles Ellicott is careful that it is not lifted to strike but to give emphasis to an oath, whose substance the histories supply; Wesley calls it dreadful and irrevocable. Ellicott also observes that the next verse is evidently copied from a prophet, with his verb scatter replaced by the overthrow just used — an error, if it is one, as old as the Greek version. Keil and Delitzsch pass over this stretch, running their quotation from the murmuring to the sins in Canaan before commenting.

At Baal-peor the interest turns on what was worshipped and what was eaten. Gill sets the name among its fellows, the Baal of the Egyptians and of the Ekronites, this one Moab's, and traces the occasion to Balaam's advice that the women of Moab draw Israel first into fornication and then into idolatry. Adam Clarke records the ancient renderings and takes the sacrifices of the dead for sacrifices of dead men, since most heathen idols were men deified after death, many execrated in life. Ellicott disagrees: the phrase means the sacrifices of a dead divinity, Baal-peor himself, and the parallel is the expression used elsewhere of the carcases of idols, so no allusion to rites for the dead need be sought here. Spurgeon leaves it open, allowing they may have joined in rites meant to open correspondence with departed spirits; but his moral is different — a false way of worship leads before long to a false god, and he names the ritualism of his own day as the first step.

The act of Phinehas is approved by all, but on different grounds. Gill has him rising when no one else would and taking on himself the office of a magistrate, and is careful what the commendation means: no works done by the best of men can justify them, much less one action, so what is said is that God esteemed the deed righteous, stopped the plague, and gave the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, putting it beyond those who would call the act rash or cruel for allowing no time for repentance. Wesley says simply that it was accepted and rewarded as an act of justice and piety. Ellicott reports that the versions do not even agree on the verb, one rendering it prayed and another appeased.

At the waters of strife Spurgeon asks whether they will never have done — the scene changes, the sin continues, and since they had mutinied over water before, the repetition made the offence sevenfold. He is gentle with Moses, who after forty years was wearied out and hopeless of their improving, and whose temper gave way; can we wonder, since he was man and not God. Clarke takes the two Hebrew words for the lapse to mean he stammered, transported with anger. Gill insists the fault was not only Moses's but belonged to those who provoked him, which is why it is mentioned. Ellicott alone reads the pronoun differently: the natural sense is Moses's spirit, as the ancient versions took it, but usage favours God's — the people rebelled against his Spirit. He adds that the usual account of Moses's offence is partial: a comparison of the narratives suggests he was excluded less for calling them rebels than for a momentary lapse into their own despairing temper.
34:
Matthew Henry marks the transition: the mercies that settled them in Canaan made no more durable impression than those that fetched them out of Egypt, and the first step of apostasy was sparing the nations they were commanded to destroy, under a pretence of pity. C.H. Spurgeon is harsher about the motive — sloth, cowardice or sinful complacency sheathed the sword too soon — and turns it on his readers: we make alliances of peace where we ought to proclaim war to the knife, pleading temperament, habit or necessity of circumstance as an apology for a sanctification at best very partial. John Gill traces the mixing through covenants, trade and intermarriage, noting the irony that they came to serve the idols of the very people dispossessed for serving them. Adam Clarke draws the lesson from the word itself, rendered their labours or griefs, named from the pains of making the images, the labour of worshipping them, and the grief the judgments brought.

The word rendered devils is disputed. Clarke insists on demons and makes a point of the number: the devil is never plural in Scripture, there being one devil though many demons. Charles Ellicott takes the word for lords, chosen to carry the heathen divine names, and traces its Arabic cognate to the title that became the Cid in Spain and survives in the Moorish word for my lord. John Wesley reads it plainly: they did not worship God as they pretended but devils in their idols, the spirits supposed to inhabit the images being evil ones. Gill collects the philology and leaves it open: a derivation from a root meaning to waste and destroy, a rabbinic objection that this needs different pointing, and a proposal from an Arabic root meaning to rule, these demons being princes reckoned among the gods. On the blood that follows, Ellicott notes that child sacrifice was inherent in Canaanite and Phoenician practice, Carthage being notorious for it two centuries after Christ.

The judgment and deliverances are handled briefly. Gill fills in the history from Judges on both sides, naming the oppressing nations and delivering judges; Clarke observes that the whole book is a history of this people's rebellions and deliverances, and reads the kindled wrath as a fire answering that with which they had inflamed themselves before their idols. Spurgeon finds the turn at their cry very godlike: one would have thought the Lord would shut out the prayer of those who had shut their ears against him, but his fiercest wrath toward his own people is a temporary flame while his love burns on for ever. Gill is exact about which covenant is remembered — not theirs, who promised to do all the Lord commanded and did not, but his. Ellicott glosses the pity of their captors as literally giving them for companions, a phrase found in Solomon's prayer.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the prayer near the end as the goal toward which the whole psalm has struggled by way of self-accusation and praise of God's faithfulness, reading the rare verb that closes it as meaning that we may account ourselves happy in being able to praise him. On the benediction they and Ellicott agree it is the doxology closing the fourth book, and both read its quotation in Chronicles as evidence about the Psalter's assembly: Ellicott takes it to show the book was complete by then, if not the collection, while Delitzsch describes the chronicler as one who joins passages like mosaic-work, inserting an indispensable rivet and turning the direction that all the people say Amen into a historical statement that they said it. Clarke renders the great phrase as from the hidden term to the hidden term, quoting an old psalter: without beginning and without ending. Spurgeon closes on the impossibility of what is commanded: if all nations united in the acclaim it would still fall short of his deserts.
